utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Margetts, you may proceed to examine the witness, but before doing so, Mr. Egrlic, I'd like to remind you that you gave a solemn declaration at the beginning of your testimony, and that solemn declaration still binds you. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before I proceed with the questions, I'd just like to address Exhibit P233.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We had a discussion in private session in relation to that exhibit yesterday. I'd just like to advise the Court that we do not wish to tender this exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It was tendered in a previous proceeding and it was not tendered under seal in that proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's, then, clear. Mr. Registrar, you made note of it, I take it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would Exhibit P233 be able to be returned to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I ask you again to return to the entry for 5 February 1992 in this diary. And if at this time you could refer to the entry for item 3, which is headed "The attitude towards the referendum." And you'll find that this entry commences on the page that is headed "4 January." Mr. Egrlic, in this entry, there are instructions set out in relation to the attitude that the SDS members are to take in respect of the referendum that was to be held in Bosnia and Herzegovina relating to the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the entries states that "The SDS members are to care about the referendum as much as about last year's snow." In Kljuc, can you describe the attitude that the Serbian people took to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's something fundamental that's wrong with this whole approach of putting diaries in front of a witness. This is another person's diary altogether. It -- it appears clear, because no such question has been asked -- it has got nothing whatever to do with this witness. He had no hand whatever in this diary. He's confirmed he never saw it before he came to this Tribunal. To put somebody else's diary before a witness in this way is effectively no different from counsel, for example, preparing a note of the points that appear in the diary and feeding that note to the witness. And we see inherent in the question that's been asked, it is in effect a disguised, but a very thinly disguised, leading question, because it puts the entry in the diary and invites the witness. The questions can simply be put as questions and this diary should be discarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need to deal with these matters in the most efficient way possible. The more specific the question can be and the more specific the witness's answer can be, the more that is going to assist the Court in what is a very complex case. Without going into the nature of this diary, it's our submission that this diary is a document and is an instrument that can focus the witness's attention on precisely the instructions that were being implemented in Kljuc. The only evidence I seek to draw from this witness is his observations in relation to how those instructions were implemented in Kljuc, and accordingly, it's our submission that it's wholly appropriate that he respond to those matters, which were matters that were being specifically attended to in the municipality in which he was the leader of one of the principal parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand there seems to be, well, quite a fundamental difference of view. May I ask both parties: This diary, not being a diary written by this witness, Mr. Stewart, do you think that the diary could be admitted into evidence -- well, let's say even without this witness, so without his comment? I mean, because one of the consequences of saying, "Well, it's of no use to show a diary of another person to this witness," would you consider this to also be preventive from admitting it into evidence just as a document, without being introduced by the author or without being introduced by the person who seized it, who tells us where he found it? I mean, I'm trying to find out to what extent the parties differ in view as to whether or not admit this document as it was said sometimes, from the bar table, just the document. Do you consider this possible, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's possible for a diary to be admitted. For example, take the extreme case: Somebody writes a diary with a detailed account of what's happened and is dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In those circumstances, one would expect that if the diary can be properly verified, that for what it is worth, with the appropriate weight, it would be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we certainly don't suggest any extreme position such as written material can't come in. But it does have to be properly verified. So Your Honour, certainly without going into it, there are circumstances if the proper proof, verification is gone through, there are circumstances in which a diary may be admitted, for what it's worth. But the entirely separate question: Whether even in those circumstances is proper to put it in front of another witness is very much the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honour, what Mr. Margetts, who, if he'll be patient with me for one moment -- what Mr. Margetts is suggesting is in fact -- and I don't mean this disrespectfully or offensively to Mr. Margetts personally or his colleagues, but it's in effect a lazy way of doing it. That's the effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He says an efficient way, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it's -- efficient, yes. It would be very efficient simply to feed to a witness a long list of precisely the points that the Prosecution wishes to establish to make the case against Mr. Krajisnik and ask the witness to say yes or no to every one. That's the extreme end of the spectrum of efficiency. What Mr. Margetts is talking about is identifying points which are highlighted by this other person's diary and then asking this witness about those points. Well, the Prosecution can do that job. They can use this diary. They can go through. They can identify, which in effect they have to do anyway, because that's what Mr. Margetts is doing by asking these questions. They have identified the points on which they wish to ask this witness a question. What they then need to do is that small extra step of converting that point into the appropriate, balanced, non-leading question without needing then to put the actual point in the diary to the witness. It's simply an unnecessary and in fact, unfair step, and the method of identifying the points and then putting the question in a proper form is -- is perfectly efficient. It leads to a fair result and it is efficient, and it's simply a -- it's, again, no offence, the Prosecution are trying to do their job, but it is simply a lax way of doing it, and it involves this distinct element of leading, as we see from the very first question this morning, because the -- the diarist's view of this matter is very clear. That's contained in the question put to the witness. The question is no longer a neutral question. The witness is then no longer being asked the point in a neutral fashion. He has been fed, within the question, a distinct viewpoint, and this is an absolutely improper way of doing the matter, and there are points at which the simple label "efficiency" must, with respect, not be allowed to divert the questioning into a form, and the presentation of the case into a form which is not fair and not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it surprises us that Mr. Stewart has raised this issue this morning, given the discussions that we had in private session yesterday. The issue of this diary coming into evidence is merely an issue of the order of proof. Secondly, I haven't heard from the Defence that they're going to object to this diary being admitted into evidence from the bar table. But one way or the other, either this will be admitted from the bar table, it can be admitted with evidence from those that seized it, it can be admitted in evidence from witnesses we anticipate to bring before the Court. So the question of this diary going into evidence is something that I think we should leave to one side. In terms of this being a lax way of asking the question, or being reduced to merely an issue of efficiency, that's not the case at all, in our submission. It's precisely for the reasons of fairness that we are putting the precise instructions in the precise words, as they are recorded in evidence that will be before this Court. That means there is no input from Prosecution into the interpretation of those words, and it means that the witness is responding precisely to the evidence that this Court will have to consider in relation to the instructions that were given to the lower levels. So where Mr. Stewart says this is not neutral, in fact that's the very essence of the reason we're putting it this way, so that we can ensure absolute neutrality and absolute accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the Chamber considers the best way of dealing with the matter the following: Let's just take the example we just had. You'd like to see whether what the witness experienced in reality is consonant with what has been written on paper. Often it may well be possible to ask this witness, without specific reference to the relevant page of the diary, to ask, for example, what the attitude was in -- in view of a plebiscite or a referendum or whatever. You could have asked him, and there's nothing then against drawing the attention of the Chamber to what extent this supports certain parts of this diary. If the witness would have said, "Well, they paid as much attention as the rain in spring," then of course you could have confronted the witness with the existence of evidence, and then we start from the point of view that one way or the other this diary could be admitted into evidence and then say, "There is evidence which says so and so and so, would that contradict your answer and to what extent and what facts make you think that you should pay as much attention as spring -- as rain in spring rather than snow in winter or snow in summer?" That's the best way to deal with it, because it gives you an opportunity to go back to the precise wording of the diary and to instruct -- to give the diary, but not after first having -- having given an opportunity to the witness to respond spontaneously to the issue where you have a specific portion of the diary in the back of your mind. But the Chamber very much would like to know what you had in the back of your mind once the witness has answered the question, so that we can find it, and if there's any need to further explore the matter, since there is some -- since the answers are not congruent with what is written on paper -- and let's not forget what's written on paper is not what happened in reality; these are two different things. So to confront the witness, "This and this instructions were given," that of course doesn't automatically mean that they were implemented, that they were visibly implemented, and we'd first like to know what the witness recalls from what he experienced in reality, and then of course the question whether this is congruent with what is in the diary is very important. If you would please proceed this way. And of course, there might be certain moments where it is more appropriate to draw the attention of specific wordings or whatever, if that becomes relevant. But please indicate that and perhaps first draw the attention of the Chamber to the part you would like to refer to and indicate, for example, by saying, "I'd like to read this or that line to the witness, or the seventh line in order to put additional questions." Then we can form ourselves an opinion on how appropriate it is, and perhaps you could put the question already and then see whether it's -- whether that question could also have been put to the witness without reading that part. So we'd like to keep some control over that. If you would please proceed this way, then we'd now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, two points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, I'm much obliged for that clear ruling. The -- the -- as far as that question is concerned, well, the witness has heard about 15 minutes debate about that particular question. Well, that's water under the bridge or last year's snow or something like that. The -- but the practical point is the witness should, we suggest, be invited to hand back the diary, if the circumstances arises Your Honour just mentioned a moment ago, where it's necessary to show it to him -- and it may often not be necessary, because it's a very short passage. He can simply be given that orally. But he should give up the copy of the diary in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's say that in order to prevent a lot of walking up and down for the usher that the diary that's in front of you, you may consult it on the pages when instructed to do so, and then -- I mean, the front page is not really dangerous, is it, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he -- with respect, he must, please, put the diary somewhere where he -- it's right in front of him at the moment. But if it can be put to one side -- if it is conspicuously put to one side, then that's quite satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he doesn't consult the -- the diary when -- we'll look at that. So the diary you have in front of you or whether it's a bit to the left or a bit to the right is not the main issue. You should not consult it unless instructed to do so. And then we'll tell you exactly what page to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, he could, for example, perfectly easily just put it on the ELMO to the left of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a very practical matter. If it's closed and if he doesn't consult it, that's sufficient. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of Your Honour's ruling, I won't need to refer the witness to the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then it may be returned. You said there were two issues, Mr. Stewart. The second one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I mentioned the first. I just commented about that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was point number one. Point number two was the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the ruling is for future questions, if Mr. Margetts thinks the question to be of importance, he may put it again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that the witness will not have the diary before him and the witness will not be asked questions about the diary. But for the Trial Chamber's benefit, I'd be pleased if the copy of the diary could remain before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have it -- at least, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask -- I'm sorry to be on my feet again. But Mr. Margetts is quite right. And in response to Your Honours' questions, we -- we simply reserve our position as to this diary and its admissibility, because at the moment no application has been made, therefore no objection could possibly be raised, and we reserve our position. But in advance of this diary coming into evidence, to invite the Trial Chamber to be looking at points in the diary as we go through does seem to be rather cart before horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly the reason why I -- my first question to the parties was whether they considered that the diary as such, apart from this witness, could be -- could be admitted into evidence. You reserve your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the reservation made by the Defence, Mr. Margetts, yes, perhaps I'll give you an opportunity first to...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stewart has come very late with this suggestion that he may or may not object to this diary. This diary has been admitted from the bar table in another Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In another trial. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: There's -- there is an affidavit I can produce to the Court from an investigator who seized it. There is a 92 bis application pending in respect of the admission of the transcript of a witness who referred to this diary and was able to substantiate it. If it was the case that the Defence intended honestly and truly to object to this diary, then it's my submission that the appropriate time for the Defence to indicate that was when this diary was introduced yesterday. We've now spent quite some time in private session talking about this diary. We've spent another 15 or so minutes this morning talking about this diary. It seems to me that Mr. Stewart needs to state his position clearly: Does he object to this or not? He's had ample time to consider it. And the way this has proceeded, in our view, is wholly inadequate. And if Mr. Stewart now wishes to reserve his position, that's something that he probably won't change. And there's no point debating it further. But in future, it would be beneficial for these proceedings if the Defence was to state their position clearly and precisely at the appropriate time. And we will save a lot of time in these proceedings. That said, in light of Mr. Stewart's statement that he reserves his position on this diary, it's not our application that the diary be before the Trial Chamber. We're content to proceed with the questioning of this witness and possibly at a later time we'll assist the Trial Chamber with indicating the potential link between this diary and the evidence that was elicited from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, does the author to be dead in order for this diary to be admitted? I take it that you have knowledge of where it comes from and that, as the Prosecution says, affidavits can be provided. You said you reserve your right. Is that to say that you have not finally made up your mind, or do you oppose to it or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it means exactly that. When Mr. Margetts said he didn't think my position would change -- of course my position may change if at the moment I'm reserving my position. I won't reserve my position forever; I can't do that. The position is, Your Honour, that when a -- when an application is made in the proper way for admission of this diary, then my position will no longer be reserved. I shall have to take a position in respect of that, and that is -- that's where I stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The 92 bis applications for the moment, we understood had been expressed -- had been deferred at the express request of the Prosecution anyway. But so far as the -- what we how often do on the Defence side, Your Honour, is we think about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what happens, and we discuss them amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the question is whether time had been sufficient until now to think it over, and of course if you insist on such an application to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I thought -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- we'll allow Mr. Margetts to quote from the diary. Whether we read it or not is a different matter, but to quote from the diary if there's any need to confront the witness with the content of this diary. To say if, witness, if someone would have written, and then you can take the exact line relevant and you can confront the witness with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just comment? I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stewart. We are not commenting. We are continuing now with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I submit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- it really -- it follows from everything I said. It is simply unnecessary and inappropriate for any quotation from this diary to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there has been a ruling on that. Mr. Margetts will start his questions without reference to any part of the -- but he may quote or -- parts of the diary if needed, and then later on I take it, Mr. Margetts, that you'll write down where questions answered by the witness are related to certain parts of the -- of this diary, and if there was no need for further questions, that you'll indicate, when tendering the diary, as a matter of -- you said you intended to tender the diary. You'll clearly indicate in the following order, this question to witness Egrlic related to that part of this diary. And if there's any need, in view of the answer of the witness, to further explore any discrepancies between the diary and the answer of the witness, then you may quote those parts of the diary relevant. So either we find later what link there is if the diary is admitted into evidence, or we find it now by your quotations, if there's any further need to explore the matter at this very moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one clarification in respect of my comments regard Mr. Stewart's position. When I referred to his position, I wasn't referring to his position as to the admission or non-admission of this document. I was referring to the fact that he currently reserves his position on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That was the issue I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, do you recall the referendum that was scheduled for the end of February, early March in Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In Kljuc, what was the response of the Serbian people to this referendum?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian people did not vote in the referendum; whereas, the Bosniak and the Croatian peoples did. And those citizens who wanted to vote in the referendum could do so and did so, and they voiced their opinion on the question that was proposed in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As at 5 February 1992, were there discussions in Kljuc in relation to the issue of whether a war option would be pursued or peace would be pursued?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This issue was not addressed in that particular way. There was never any discussion about war versus peace, at least in not so many words. This issue was never treated in that way. However, judging by the situation that was -- that existed in Kljuc and some activities, the security situation deteriorated by the day, and one could easily conclude that this situation might escalate and turn into an even more serious case of order being disrupted in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yesterday we referred to a number of documents and announcements that were written by yourself and Mr. Omer Filipovic. In those documents and announcements, you referred to a war policy being pursued. In your previous answer, you spoke about the escalation of events. Did you perceive that that war policy that you referred to was escalating in the Municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because during the month of February, in addition to the obvious armament of the population, units of the former JNA were stationed in the compound of the former forestry company, and this compounded the situation in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, in February 1992, there was discussion in the media in relation to the issue of the declaration of the autonomous region. And Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond one of the issues that was discussed was the issue of the application of what was referred to as the ethnic principle as one of the criterions for the division of Bosnia into autonomous regions. In the context of the division of Bosnia, how did you see that ethnic principle applied in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that Kljuc had been annexated [as interpreted] to the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina by the will of the Serbian people. This is where we recognised this ethnic principle, given the fact that the will of other ethnic groups residing in the area was neither listened to or respected. The other municipalities around Kljuc where the Serbian population was in a majority also took such decisions, and their municipalities were linked up with the autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present to the witness the next exhibit. It's the first one listed on the second page of the exhibit list, and it's dated 18 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P234 and P234.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, this is a handwritten document which purports to be the minutes of a meeting of the Municipal Board of the SDS on 18 February 1992. If I could refer you to the second page of this document and in particular an entry which is below the halfway mark of the document and is in relation to item 2 on the agenda. And this is a report presented by Veljko Kondic. Could I ask you to read that entry in respect of the report presented by Veljko Kondic wherein he refers to the issue of regionalisation of local communes and, secondly, he speaks about problems relating to the location of the JNA in Laniste, and then I'll ask you some questions in respect of that. Mr. Egrlic, in this report, Mr. Kondic states that the SDA has raised the issue of regionalisation of local communes. Can you comment in relation to whether or not that is an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement is not correct. The SDA raised the issue of organising the Bosnian Municipality of Kljuc, to which I testified yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Secondly, he speaks about problems relating to the location for the JNA in Laniste. You've mentioned before that army units came to Kljuc. Did you observe army units at Laniste?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And there was a discussion on this issue at a meeting of the National Defence Council. Representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party wanted to see JNA units which had been withdrawing from Knin to be stationed at Laniste. We, on the other hand, were of the opinion that there was no need for that and that such a development could only instill fear amongst the citizens. However, since the SDS had a majority in the council, they voted in favour of these units coming and being stationed at Laniste. After that, the workers protested because Laniste is a forestry company compound and the workers of the company Sipad Kljuc had their workshops there, their restaurant, and other facilities. As from then on, all of these facilities were occupied by the troops, so the workers did not have any place where they could prepare for their work in the forests. Our role was to calm the situation down. On one occasion, we were asked to come together to Laniste in order to deal with the situation. On that occasion, I saw JNA units stationed at Laniste; I also saw that they were armed. There were cannons lined up facing the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who did you go to Laniste with?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went together with the Secretary for National Defence and Jovo Banjac, who was the president of the Municipal Assembly. We wanted to deal with the situation and to stop the workers' strike. They -- the workers did not concede, the conditions for their work was no longer in place once the troops were stationed there. And finally this place, Laniste, was totally closed for business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was the Secretary for National Defence a Serb by the name of Slobodan Jurisic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan Jurisic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And about -- or around about when did you go to Laniste?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been around the 20th February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I refer you back to the first page of the document that is before you, and in particular I refer you to item 4, which is listed on the list of agenda items. This item refers to: "The organisation of the Territorial Defence, enhancement of combat readiness of the population." Did you observe that a Serbian Territorial Defence was being organised as at February 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was permanent as of the second half of 1991 onwards. However, as of the beginning of 1992, this was even stepped up. There were constant mobilisation calls to the ranks of the Territorial Defence. The number and presence of soldiers in the territory of the municipality increased. Every citizen could observe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How did the arrival of the army at Laniste make the Bosniaks in Kljuc feel?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before that, people were scared. And once the JNA arrived at Laniste, there was even more anxiety among the people and the fear for their security increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In April 1992, was there any change in the capacity of the people in Kljuc to receive radio communications? And I'm referring to radio broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as radio programmes are concerned, they were still broadcast. People did listen to the radio. The only thing that changed was the management of the radio. Before that, the editor-in-chief was Mr. Asmir Burzic, who was replaced sometime in April by a gentleman who was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What nationality was Mr. Burzic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I've finished with the document that's before you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I'd now like to present Mr. Egrlic with the next exhibit, which is the second one on the second page. The exhibit that's dated 29 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this document would have number 235, I take, and the English translation, 235.1?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, these are the handwritten notes of the meeting of the SDS Municipal Board on the 29th of April, 1992. I'd like to refer you to a discussion that took place in respect of item 1 on the agenda, which was "Consideration of the security situation in the municipality." And in particular, I'd like you -- I'd like to refer you to the comments made by Vinko Kondic that commence in the bottom three lines of the first page and run through to almost the middle of the second page. Just before I do that, I'd just like to ask you: Who is Mr. Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Kondic was the Chief of the Police Administration in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was he the brother of Mr. Veljko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not his brother. They were related.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you have an association with Mr. Vinko Kondic prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had contacts with him. We worked together in the same construction company, the Sana of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Omer Filipovic have contacts with Vinko Kondic prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. They were friends. Their families were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Over what period of time did you observe the relationship between Mr. Omer Filipovic and Mr. Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war and during 1991, and as much as I can remember, this continued in 1992, up to April sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Returning to the document before you. The opening comments from Mr. Vinko Kondic are that "The situation in Kljuc Municipality is unbearably calm." Do you have any comment you'd like to make in regard to that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in a way -- how shall I put it? In a way, this is a mocking comment on the situation, as if they were expecting some unrest and found it strange that there were none, that there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you say, "They were expecting some unrest," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were many occasions when citizens were upset and they had probably been expecting citizens to react to the shooting occasioned by the departure of fighters to the Croatian battlefield and found it strange probably that people did not react in the way they had expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So as at 29 April 1992, the situation in Kljuc was calm, was peaceful, there was no reaction to the shooting.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Despite these initial observations, Mr. Kondic continues, and he says, "We cannot overcome the situation in a peaceful way."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is really quite a serious error in the translation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The word in Serbian, I understand, is at the beginning of that sentence, "We cannot overcome," it goes, "Mi nastojimo." And nastojimo, n-a-s-t-o-j-i-m-o, it's something that anybody with knowledge of the Latin language will see that it's "we," it means, "We are trying to overcome this situation in a peaceful way." So this translation could hardly be wronger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two issues first, whether there's any dispute possible about what the text says in B/C/S because it's handwriting. You always have to be very careful with that. And the second issue is how it then should be translated as written. Could a copy of this document be put on the ELMO and then specifically the B/C/S portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask who is going to be invited to rule on this? Because it's not really a matter for the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course not. It's a way -- it's a way of all interpreters to be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. That's what I was concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you -- I take it that it's on the third page, the Vinko Kondic, the second -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Obviously I'm getting my information from Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I do not expect you to have taken a B/C/S course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will appear on the second page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on the second page of the B/C/S, the upper part. Could the -- let's first see whether it's clear enough on the video monitor. Yes, is this readable for the booth? I invite one of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then in the translation, we find a line which says, "Serbs are the majority population in Kljuc." The relevant part is the sentence prior to that one. Could perhaps it first be read to see and also to give Ms. Cmeric an opportunity to check whether there's any discussion possible about what the B/C/S says. Could the B/C/S booth read aloud that sentence prior to the one, "Serbs are the majority population in Kljuc." Now, I have to change ... Ms. Cmeric, were you able to follow the reading and do you agree that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honours. I just couldn't find the right channel. Is that the B/C/S channel, number 6? I don't hear any translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It might be 5. Oh, no, that's French. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number 6 is the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it perhaps be read again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, the reading is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reading is correct. Could we -- could we, then, please receive the translation of the line just read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: English booth: We are trying to deal with or overcome the situation in a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be an error in translation, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is an official CLSS translation, and we will send -- send that back for amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- we understand they don't mean they're trying to deal with the situation in the booth in a peaceful way, which is what it -- which is how it sounded. Although, we hope that is the position, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just the way it came across, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. There's never any competition in the booth, as far as I am aware of. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, consistent with that corrected translation, there's a reference in the last sentence of Mr. Kondic's report which states "We decided not to change our insignia. We must be wise, bring everything to a conclusion without war and achieve the final goal." At that time, what did you understand to be the final goal of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from all the preceding activities, one could infer that the final goal was to create a parastate in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be annexed to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I refer you to the comments which appear just before the middle of this second page, and they're comments attributed to Jovanka Cvijic. And this person refers to the refusal of the Muslims to sign the pledge of loyalty. As at 29 April 1992, had you been asked to sign a pledge of loyalty? And if so, what was the nature of that pledge?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They required all Bosniaks who worked in administration agency in -- in agencies in the police department and in senior positions in enterprises to sign a pledge of loyalty -- or rather, a declaration of loyalty to the Republika Srpska. That meant that the citizens of Kljuc municipality would also in this way accept this new parastate in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And skipping the comments of Vinko Kondic and moving to the comments of Veljko Kondic on that second page. He states that the power in Kljuc is really at the hands of the Serbs. As at 29 April 1992, is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a correct description, because power was in fact in the hands of the Serbs, even in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. That's all my questions in respect of that document. In the course of reviewing the comments of Mr. Vinko Kondic in that previous document, there was a reference to the change of the insignia and division of the police. Can you describe to the Court the nature of the request that was made to the Muslims in regard to the change of the insignia and the various meetings you had with representatives at the municipal level and other levels in relation to the proposed change of the insignia.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their demand to change the existing insignia and accept new insignia was especially prominent in the ranks of the police, considering that in the period 1991 to May 1992 the police was a mixed force. The Bosniak policemen were asked to sign not only the declaration of loyalty to the Republika Srpska but also to sign a statement confirming their acceptance of new uniforms and new insignia on those uniforms, which they refused. They refused because the new insignia were not in conformity with the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina had not adopted any law or enactment on the change of insignia. It was done instead by the leadership of the SDS and the autonomous authorities in Banja Luka, and they -- it was they who wanted Bosniaks to accept them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At the municipal level, who did you discuss the issue of the change of insignia with and what was said in these discussions?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this demand was raised, to change the insignia, they sought approval from the political organisations, the SDA and the MBO. They wanted us to suggest to the policemen in some way that they should accept the new insignia; however, we did not wish to do that because the insignia had been changed in circumvention of the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the new insignia represented symbols only of the Serbian people, and therefore disregarded the rights of Bosniak policemen, who were until then part of the police force in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you refer to "they," who were the representatives of the Serb people that you discussed this with?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Vinko Kondic, as Chief of the Police Administration; Veljko Kondic, as president of the Municipal Organisation of SDS of Kljuc; and Mr. Banjac, as president of the Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How did they explain the reasons for the change of insignia to you, and what did they say in respect of their role in arriving at this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kljuc municipality, we managed to stall on that issue for quite a long time because there was a certain degree of tolerance on the part of the representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party; however, eventually they said that they were not the ones who had the main say in the matter. They said that it was higher authorities who really decided on that, and they told us to visit Banja Luka and the Centre of Security Services, headed by Stojan Zupljanin, and they said that if Mr. Zupljanin should agree that the insignia remain, as they used to be until then, they would not object. So that meeting with Mr. Zupljanin was scheduled, and we went to Banja Luka to have talks with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who went to Banja Luka to talk to Mr. Zupljanin, and about when did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and the late Omer Filipovic went to Banja Luka, together with Jovo Banjac, Vinko Kondic, and Veljko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did this meeting take place in early May?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held on the 2nd or 3rd May. I don't know exactly. But the outcome of the meeting was negative; we did not reach any agreement there. Mr. Zupljanin, you could say, laughed in our faces, saying that it was a done deal. He gave each of us a beret with new insignia, telling us to take it back and show it to the Bosniak policemen. He said we should tell them to accept it because it looks quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin said it was a done deal. What did you think he meant by those words?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We understood him to mean that he was not able to decide on that one way or another, that some other people or other organs were the ones who decided on that, and that we were talking to a man who was unable to help us in any way in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Zupljanin was the head of the regional police in Banja Luka, yet from what you said, he didn't have the power to decide in respect of this matter. From his answers to you, who did you think had made the decision for the change in insignia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only surmise. But generally speaking, symbols such as the national flag --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The answer follows -- in some ways the problem follows from the question. We've had this point many, many times before, actually. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can -- I'll give some instruction to Mr. Margetts, and if there's any reason to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to make any further submissions, you may do so. Mr. Margetts, the questions are almost invitations for speculation. Could you please ask the witness if he interpreted certain words in a certain way, what those words then exactly were. And how, based on what he heard, he drew these conclusions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you drew the conclusion when you were speaking to Mr. Zupljanin that some other people or other organs were the ones who decided on the issue of the change of insignia. Can you recall precisely what it was in Mr. Zupljanin's words or manner or presentation to you that resulted in you forming that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that he told us that it was a done deal and there was nothing he could do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: After you left the meeting, how did you travel back to Kljuc and who did you travel with?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We travelled in two passenger cars; I and late Omer Filipovic and Vinko Kondic took one car, and Veljko Kondic, Jovo Banjac, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter forgot the third person --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- took the other car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please again tell us who the third person was. You said Veljko Kondic, Jovo Banjac, and ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one car travelled I and Omer Filipovic and Vinko Kondic, and in the second car, Jovo Banjac and Veljko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No third person in the other car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just the driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As you travelled in the vehicle with Mr. Kondic, did you discuss what had taken place at this meeting and what would then follow from the comments of Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What did Mr. Kondic say?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had been saying even way back that it had to happen because the adjacent municipalities effected this before the Kljuc Municipality and the Kljuc Municipality had to make these changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two very short exhibits that I'd like to present to the witness. I'm mindful of the time, but I would be able to do that in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take those minutes and then have a break. So first, if they're really short. I take it that within five, six minutes we could deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, and we'll then have a break until 11.00 later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could be presented with the two documents which are appearing as the fifth and the sixth -- oh, sorry, that is the fourth and the fifth documents on the second page of the exhibit list. They are dated respectively 4th May and 5th May. And if the witness could be given the 5th May document first and have the 4th May document placed on the table next to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 5th May document will have number 236 for the original and 236.1 for the English translation. And the 4th of May document will have P237 for the original and 237.1 for the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, the document you have before you is an order of the president of the Council for National Defence, Jovo Banjac. And pursuant to the second item of this order, it imposes a curfew in the Municipality of Kljuc. Do you recall seeing this order around the 5th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the session of the council, which adopted the decision to issue this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was your position in respect of the curfew?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asserted and substantiated with fact that there was no reason to introduce this curfew to restrict the movement of people and put up obstacles in streets, which would intimidate citizens even more. But they contradicted us, saying that they wished to stand in the way of people coming back from battlefields carrying weapons, that they wanted to prevent the citizens from being disturbed, that they wanted to run checks Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond on the movement of people, and they voted in favour of introducing this curfew, regardless of our objection, and following the curfew, following the decision on the curfew, they blocked completely all intersections and introduced this 10.00 p.m. to 5.00 a.m. curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was the late Mr. Omer Filipovic present at this meeting, and did he also oppose the curfew?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He attended as vice-president of the Municipality, and he was also opposed to this, together with all the other members of the council who were Bosniaks. In our view, there was really no need for this curfew, not from our standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I refer to the document, and it states in the preamble that "This order is made pursuant to the decision by the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Was there any discussion at this meeting in relation to any order that had come from the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no specific mention of any order that had arrived, but they justified the introduction of the curfew by saying they wished to have control over the armed soldiers who were present around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did they say that they had arrived at this decision by their own volition or that, alternatively, they felt bound to implement this decision?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They claimed they had to implement this decision for the reasons I've stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I've finished with that document. If you could refer to the document that's on your left. This is a reasonably poor copy of the document, and I'm referring to the document that's been marked P237 and is a decision of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, dated 4 May 1992. But could you refer to item 4, which is the fourth paragraph down, under the heading, "The decision."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, in view of the quality of the document, could you please first invite the witness to read that paragraph to see whether at all there's any text he could say something about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, that paragraph I've indicated, could you please read that out to the Court just to verify that the reproduction is sufficient to draw your comment on.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is not visible in all places, so I cannot read it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, wouldn't it be then a good moment to have our break for 25 minutes and upon return to produce perhaps a copy which could be read? Because there must be somewhere some copy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll attempt to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we resume, Mr. Margetts, I'd like to address the Prosecution in respect of the response to the motion filed by the -- I think, Mr. Hannis, it's more your cup of tea. The Prosecution has asked 14 days, the normal delay, for responding to the motion on the translations. The Chamber would very much like to hear, I would say, the global position, well, let's say, by tomorrow. By "global position," I mean by the -- without too many details, whether the Prosecution has made up its mind already whether to oppose against granting the motion or partially oppose or supports or whatever. The Chamber would very much like to receive that also in order to determine whether the full 14 days should be granted or not or whether -- well, it's important for us to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could file something that soon, just advising you of our general position, with regard to the motion. We would like to have additional time to file a fuller response, because the two senior trial attorneys on this case, Mr. Tieger and Mr. Harmon, are out of the country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- and we need to contact them and consult with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do understand. But a global position, even if it would have -- would have been done orally. It's not necessarily done in writing. But I then take it that you could explain your position in not more than two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, we will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we expect that, then, to be done tomorrow in the afternoon, if possible. Mr. Margetts, please proceed. Oh, yes. Perhaps you'd first provide the witness with a legible copy of the 4th of May, that's 237, the original. Yes. Mr. Egrlic, could you please give it another attempt to read paragraph 4 of this document provided to you now in a -- at least, a better copy. We'll see whether it's legible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 4, it says: "A curfew is being introduced in the entire territory between 2200 hours and 0500 hours, except for those with official authorities issued either by the police, the military police, or the Serbian Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's only one small thing in the oral translation now, whether it says "for everyone," was missing. Could I ask whether that appears in the original or not, as read by the -- perhaps we could ask Ms. Cmeric to give the -- the position of the Defence. In the written translation, we find "for everyone," which was not part of the oral translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the original doesn't read -- there's no word "everyone" in the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't make that much of a difference, but I just wanted to check. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, referring to paragraph 4, as you have just read it into the record, is that consistent with the curfew that was introduced on the 5th of May in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. That's all I have in respect of that document. Now, Mr. Egrlic, we understand that certain events occurred on the 7th of May, 1992, and we will address those events. I'd just like to ask you a couple of small questions in relation to matters preceding the 7th of May, 1992. We referred to the change of the management of the radio station in April 1992. Prior to 7 May 1992, had there been any other dismissals of Bosniaks from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bosniaks were dismissed from the financial transaction institution. Rifat Silajdzic was dismissed from there, from the SDK, and this is the only dismissal I am aware of that happened before the 7th of May. After the 7th of May, however, everybody else was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Prior to the 7th of May, what were the reasons given for the dismissals of the gentleman from the radio and gentleman from the SDK?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were told that since there had been a takeover in Kljuc, they had to be replaced by individuals from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, what happened on the 7th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, flags were put up on the buildings of all public institutions. Those were the flags of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The insignia on the police uniforms were changed, and it was said officially that Bosniaks, given the fact that they had not signed a document pledging loyalty to the new state, those who were employed in state bodies, that they could leave -- they were urged to leave the municipality building and pretend that they were on holiday, and if they were needed, they would be called back to work. All this was accompanied by the entry of the Serbian army, units which were composed of reservists from the territories of Sanski Most and Prijedor municipalities; namely, units which were part of the 6th Krajina Brigade and which had already had control of all the roads in the municipality and the most important points around the town, as well as all the institutions in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present two exhibits to the witness. The first exhibit is the sixth exhibit on the second page, the one that's dated 8 May 1992 in the exhibit list and has the ERN for translation 01107351. And the second one I'd like to introduce is one that's further down the page on the exhibit -- the second page of the exhibit list, and it's got the date 18 May 1992 and has the ERN on the first page, 01906806. If they could be presented to the witness and if, in fact, the second document I've referred to could be presented first and numbered first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, would you please first deal with the 18th of May document. Mr. Margetts, the 8th of May document, I do not find the date, apart from in the first line saying that "The Crisis Staff of Kljuc Municipality informs and --" oh, yesterday. Yes, the 7th of May, makes it the 8th of May; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the clarification in respect of that document. In fact, the date ascribed to this first document I'm referring to is an error. There is no reference on this document, as far as I can see, to 18 May, in fact, there is a handwritten annotation which is "18-05/92," which I think is the number of the order itself, not a reference to a date, and the context of the document indicates that it is not a document produced on the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it could not be the 18th of May, since if the soldiers still have to be provided a cooked dinner on the 8th of May, then you couldn't decide that on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. So we make that an undated document. And then also in the description, it's an order by Branko Basara without a date, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could have numbers for these exhibits, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the second one first, the undated first. Mr. Registrar, I think we are at P238; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the order gets the exhibit number P238 and its English translation gets the exhibit number P238.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the public announcement gets Exhibit Number P239, and its English translation, P239.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, in your answer to the previous question, you referred to the 6th Brigade. Can you refer to the document before you, and do you note that at the top of that document it refers to the 6th Partisan Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Is this the unit of the JNA you were referring to as the unit that entered Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, can I refer you to the bottom of that order and the entry numbered 9, which continues on over the page, and the subparagraphs of that order 9(a), (b), (c), and (d). In respect of the deployment of the platoons and companies referred to in paragraph 9, is that consistent with what you observed in Kljuc on the 7th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I've finished with that document. If you could take a look at the second document, which is the public announcement. In particular, I'd like to refer you to the fifth paragraph on the first page, which is the second paragraph from the bottom on the first page. And this paragraph states that "Since the Kljuc Municipality reached the decision in respect of joining the Autonomous Region and that this is part of the territory of the Serbian Republic, the Kljuc Municipality will automatically be obliged to implement laws and decisions reached by the Assembly of the Serbian Republic and the Assembly of the Autonomous Region." Mr. Egrlic, can you comment on this public announcement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This announcement for the public is addressing the citizens in order to explain what had happened on the 7th of May, 1992, in light of the fact that the citizens were astounded by the developments. This is the way things were explained to them, an attempt to explain things to the citizens, and to indicate to them where the Municipality of Kljuc would be as of then on within this new system and organisation. This also served to show that the citizens would be guaranteed all of their rights and freedoms and that the citizens should not construe the increased presence of the troops as an attack on the freedom of any ethnic group. The citizens, Bosniaks, Croats, and some Serbs, who had not been informed of what was going on, needed an explanation because on -- on the surface whatever happened in Kljuc these days looked like an occupation of the Municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You said that the citizens were astounded with the developments. But in respect of the matter that is set out at -- in the fifth paragraph on the first page, that is, the demand for obedience to the laws of the Assembly of the Serbian People, is this not something that you had predicted and informed the citizens about from as early as September 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Secondly, you referred to the fact that the document guarantees the civil rights of persons, regardless of their national or religious affiliation. And I refer you in particular to the fourth paragraph from the bottom of the second page, which has as its condition to that guarantee of rights that "Those citizens behave correctly towards the authorities and do not disturb peace or threaten the safety of citizens and property." Subsequent to the 7th of May, 1992, were the civil rights of the Muslims respected?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not respected. First of all, their freedom of movement was limited, both in time and in space. Notebooks were introduced at the checkpoints and Bosniak citizens had to identify themselves and explain and account for their movements. The individuals who discharged certain duties in administrative bodies lost their jobs, and I cannot say that the words written here were honoured at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness the exhibit which is the third exhibit on the third page of the exhibit list, which is dated 26 June 1992, and I'd also like to show the witness the exhibit which is dated 21 July 1992 on the third page and the exhibit which is dated 3 August 1992 on the third page, and I'd like to show them in the order of the 26th June first, the 21 July second, and the 3rd August third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may distribute them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number for the document dated 26 June 1992 will be P240, and its English translation gets Exhibit Number P240.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. While Mr. Registrar is distributing further the documents, the 21st of July will be 241 and -- for the original and 241.1 for the English translation; and the document of the 3rd of August will be 242 and 242.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, do you have the document dated the 26th of June, 1992 before you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And do you see that that's a review of executive positions held by employees of Muslim nationality?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you run your eye down the list of names and tell me whether or not most or all of these people were dismissed from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The question really should be whether any of them are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It should be any of them. Because once again, these questions time after time after time point directly towards the answer that -- that counsel is looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has already said that the Muslims were dismissed from their jobs, and these are all the executive positions in the municipality where Muslims were employed, so the evidence has presupposed the question; nevertheless, if Mr. Stewart wishes to insist, I'll restate the question and I'll ask Mr. Egrlic whether any of these people were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Margetts, I'm just looking at the previous answer in respect of dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, or he could say which, if it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm trying to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am saying that I'm checking the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I was trying to be helpful. By --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't find the line where the witness said about -- I think he said that two people were fired before the 7th of May and then after the 7th of May -- I can't find the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness refers to those two people being dismissed. But in response to the question just prior to my introduction of these three documents, he stated as follows -- and it's on -- at the transcript I have before me, it's at line 42.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- 11.29.33. The witness stated: "The individuals who discharged certain duties in administrative bodies lost their jobs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was in my mind that he said something about after the 7th of May, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I refer to page 37. Yes. "After the 7th of May, everybody was dismissed." I take it that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before the 7th of May, it was just the radio and the financial institution, I think it was the DSK or DK --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: SDK, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "And then after the 7th of May, everybody was dismissed." Under those circumstances, the objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The different objection is, then, what the Americans called asked and answered, then. If that's the position, if my learned friend is saying he'll simply repeat it, if he wishes. Having got the answer they were all dismissed, why do we then need to go through a list? Because if a witness does actually mean what he says, we're simply going over the same ground again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I do understand everybody was dismissed, not to be the full 100 per cent, a large number, and the -- Mr. Margetts is now trying to clarify what exactly in more specific terms the answer would mean. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The basis for the question is -- to twofold: First of all, it's to provide further particulars to the answer that's already been given; and second of all, it's to refer specifically to a document that was produced by the Serbian government themselves, which he will then be able to give direct evidence in relation to the individuals, that they were aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- as either being employed or not employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I'll repeat the question: The document before you, dated 26 June 1992, lists various Muslim employees in executive positions. Were any of the people listed in this document dismissed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these people were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. If I could refer to the next document. I've finished with that document. That's P241.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for one clarification to the witness. You said, "They were all dismissed." It's quite a list. Did you review the list at this very moment, or did you review the list prior to giving evidence in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reviewed this list before, and I know all these people personally, and I know that all of them were dismissed from their jobs, and even though I hadn't meant to say this before, but here, in addition to the directors who were Bosniaks, there is also the name of Drasko Banjac, a Serb, who found himself on this list because he was married to a Bosniak. Therefore, they considered him unreliable and he was dismissed too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers my question. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If Mr. Egrlic could be presented with the Exhibit P240 -- 241. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, is this the decision terminating your services as chairman of the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If the -- I've finished with that document. If the witness could be shown Exhibit P242.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, does this record of 3 August 1992 refer to the departure from the municipality of your wife?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can you explain to me the circumstances of her departure and what happened to your family property following her departure.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of citizens from Kljuc municipality were driven out in the most brutal way possible; they were deported in trailer trucks, and they had to pay significant sums of money for this deportation. Before being deported, they had to pay all their utility bills and turn over their unmovable property to the municipal authorities.
