A record was made of this surrender of property, wherein a statement was taken from every citizen in question that he was renouncing his property in favour of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kljuc municipality. This is something that had to be done by everyone who had immovable property, because it was a precondition for leaving Kljuc municipality. So it was done by my wife too because she, too, had to leave Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I've finished with that document, Mr. Egrlic. Now, returning to the 7th of May, 1992, you said that the people who were not loyal to the Serbian government were removed from the municipal building. Where did you go after the 7th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 7th of May, 1992, we established an office in the Velagici local commune, in the building of the cultural hall in order to be able to have contacts with citizens, and that is where we worked from the 7th May onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And when you say "we," you are referring to yourself and Mr. Omer Filipovic and your close associates?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was this office in the settlement of Pudin Han? And if so, how far north of the city of Kljuc is Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Pudin Han, 3 kilometres or so away from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness the next exhibit, which is the document dated 12 May 1992 and is the seventh exhibit on the second page of the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would get number ...? I take it 243 for the original and 243.1 for the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, this is a decision that purports to have been made by yourself on the 12th of May, 1992. Did you make this decision and did you sign this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see a similar problem, I think, as you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond have. Mr. Margetts, the copying of the original has been done in such a way that only part of the document is visible; only the left upper part. So, therefore, signatures are not even -- could we compare your copy and -- my copy looks like this. Yes. Could you please check the copies provided. Because it has been enlarged and only part of the document is available. Could it be put on the ELMO -- could you do without it for a second?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without the original? What -- and perhaps -- what is the original that has been presented to the witness? May I have -- could you please hold the document 243 so that I can have a look at a distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have a similar problem. Could this original be replaced by the one in the hands of the usher. Mr. Usher, could you please give the other copy, the complete copy to the witness. And then after he has briefly inspected it, put it again on the ELMO so that we can all have a look at it. And since the first question was about signatures, perhaps the lower part. Mr. Usher, could you assist to -- the witness to put it on the ELMO. Mr. Egrlic, you'll see it left -- to your left-hand side, but it could also appear on the screen. The usher will help you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the signature is concerned, it says here, "President of the Executive Council, Asim Egrlic," in print. However, this signature here is not mine. The document was signed by Tihomir Dakic, vice-president of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And as at the date of this document, that is, 12 May 1992, you had no knowledge at all of this document or this decision?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge, nor was I able to make any decisions, since I did not attend at all from the 7th of May onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was another leading question. These are blatantly leading, these questions. That's -- the form of that question should be: Did you have any knowledge? Not "you had no knowledge," with a question mark tacked on the end of the answer that counsel is looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We have proceeded on the basis in this proceeding that expedition is a consideration in examination-in-chief, and given that this is a very peripheral document on a very peripheral matter, it was merely with expedition I sought to proceed. I have no comment to make about the substance of Mr. Stewart's objection, I just have a comment to make about how we can expedite the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, the question: "Did you have any knowledge?" And the answer, "no," or "You had no knowledge of it?" And the answer, "yes," is as far as time is concerned, just as expeditious. So, therefore, would you please -- where it really doesn't save time and where it's -- it's not only time, but it -- the starting point is if a question could be phrased during the examination-in-chief in such a way that it's not leading or leading to the minimal, apart from those areas that are not contested at all, then that should be chosen. And the example is a clear example with exactly the same number of words and also only one word answering that question would have created exactly the same result, and there you should certainly choose the less leading way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, as at 12 May 1992, did you know of this decision?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've finished with that document, and I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you'll provide the proper copies of 243, the original, to both Defence and Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will replace that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If Mr. Egrlic could be shown the document dated 14 May 1992, which has the translation ERN, 01106533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, could we have the original B/C/S version. I don't know whether you have another copy, but at least -- there's one in the hands of the -- of the registrar, because otherwise we are without.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if the Defence could be provided with our second copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, now, the 14th of May document will then get number 244 for the original and 244.1 for the English translation. Now, Mr. Margetts, there is some confusion. We have two documents on the list "14th of May."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. No. No, it's clear to me. There's no confusion. I'm a bit confused. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, could you refer to the first page of this document. And I'll just describe what the document is. It's the minutes of a meeting of the 14th of May between the Command of the military, Colonel Galic, and presidents of various Serbian municipalities in the region of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Mr. Egrlic, could you refer to point 5 under the listing on the first page, "Present at the meeting," and could you read the name there and tell me whether that is the president of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "President of the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc, Jovo Banjac," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you refer to paragraph 11 -- or point 11 under that heading, and could you tell me who Rajko Kalabic is.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko Kalabic was a deputy first to the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina and then to the Parliament or the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I refer you to the second page of this document and the heading "Kljuc," and note that the first words of this section read: "After the partial takeover of power." As at 14 May 1992, was that an accurate representation of the authority that was in the hands of the Serbian Municipality in Kljuc? That is, did they have total power or only partial power over the territory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had total power, even before this date when this meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder, why was the extra question put at the end is what we ask. Once again, the -- if the question had stopped, "Was that an accurate representation of the authority that was in the hands of the Serbian Municipality in Kljuc?" That would have been a shorter and more efficient question. The addition -- this is happening time after time after time -- the addition contains with it the answer that the counsel is looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can I respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Just to say that I think in the addition the only two options were presented, and accordingly, again, it was done for the reasons of the expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if they're the only two options, they don't need saying. And how it can be expedition to add unnecessary words to a question absolutely is beyond us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, there are more options. There could have been no takeover of the power at all. That would be already a third option. And, of course, the purpose of refraining from unnecessarily leading is to give an opportunity to the witness to say, "Well, partially takeover territory -- from a point of view of territory it's correct or from a point of view of" -- well, whatever. There are a lot of other options, and I -- it might well have been that the witness would have said, "No, it was not a partial but a total takeover." Fine, we would then hear that. So although it is perhaps not dramatic in respect of this, in view of what the witness said before about the power, but if you think that you should put that question to the witness in this context, where it was already another context, you could do it just as open as suggested by Mr. -- By Mr. Stewart. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, could you please refer to the third page of this document, and in particular the second-last paragraph that appears on that third page, commencing with the words, "the president of Kljuc." In the first sentence of that paragraph, it is stated that Jovo Banjac said that "In Kljuc the policy of finding a peaceful solution to the problems was still being pursued." As at 14 May 1992, was that the case?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, there was a brutal takeover, and there was nothing to the effect of a peaceful solution. We were completely peaceful, for that matter, but a peace -- finding a peaceful solution was not a topic of discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: After the 14th of May, did you meet with Jovo Banjac and discuss the situation in the municipality with him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for a meeting to see what the situation in the municipality was and to try and give the name to what was obvious. We wanted to receive information from them. At that meeting, which was held in the municipality building, there was me, there was the late Omer Filipovic, Jovo Banjac, and Veljko Kondic; however, they kept on insisting and urging us to sign the document on loyalty to the Serbian republic. We, on the other hand, as far as the municipality of Kljuc was concerned, insisted on the troops being removed with their weapons and on the life continuing the way it was before the 7th of May, before 1991, for that matter. The meeting ended without a conclusion, and we parted, and this was our last meeting with these gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Approximately what date did this meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At this meeting, what did Veljko Kondic say?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the details of what anybody said at that meeting. However, it was very clear that in that area we could not do a thing to restore things to the way they were before, and it was also clear that the Serbian people were aiming for a special state, as outlined by the high policy of the Serbian Democratic Party, and that if anything, then only that further deterioration of the relationship was in store for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Subsequent to the meeting in the municipal building, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that meeting, we went to the Lovac restaurant for a drink and an informal chat. We all had known each other for a long time, and in an informal conversation sometimes more is said than during any official meeting, and that's why we accepted the invitation for a drink and an informal chat. We thought that that might be an opportunity to convince them that there was no need for such a number of troops and military equipment in the area of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who went to the restaurant for this informal discussion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us went there: Me, Mr. Banjac, Omer Filipovic, Veljko Kondic, and Vinko Kondic, all of us who were present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How did you travel to the restaurant and with whom?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went with Mr. Banjac. I travelled in his car to the restaurant. And the others left before us in another car. They were already in the restaurant when we arrived. As he was leaving the car and locking the door, Jovo Banjac told me that they had to implement what had been outlined; namely, that people would have to be moved from this territory, that there would have to be an exodus of people from this territory. I asked him, "What kind of exodus? How do you mean moving people? How can that be carried out?" He said that, "From some territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs have to leave, and from the others, Bosniaks and Croats had to leave. So that their respective minority percentages would not be more than 5 or 6 per cent. I told him that this was plain crazy and that I couldn't understand that anybody could have conceived that in their head and that this was totally undoable. And this is how our conversation in front of the restaurant ended. Then we entered the restaurant itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Jovo Banjac said to you that they had to implement what had been outlined. What did you understand him to mean by those words?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certain by that time that the leadership of the SDS had planned the ethnic cleansing of the territory and they also planned for some of the ethnic groups to become a minority in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I refer you back to the document that is before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one intermediary question. Your answer to the last question was translated, "It was certain by that time that the leadership of the SDS had planned ...." What is the factual basis of this knowledge? Because it's a statement, rather than an observation of facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I concluded that based on the hard line offered by Mr. Banjac. It seemed to me that he personally did not share that view but that he would be willing to implement what had been outlined by the policy. According to him, the resettlement of people from certain territories was nothing but ethnic cleansing, and the establishment of mono-ethnic territories in the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer comes down to that -- it seemed to you that he personally did not share that view, so it was the view of others, and you're talking about policy. On what basis did you in your earlier answer elaborate on who those others might have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The higher leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a repetition of your answer. But on what basis you concluded that those were the -- the others and not, well, let's say, the foreign ambassadors or Greek government? I mean, others, and then you say "those." What -- on what factual basis did you conclude, as you just repeated, who those others were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I based that on the fact that Mr. Banjac always consulted with the higher bodies for all important decisions, and I believe that the resettlement of some ethnic groups from some territories was an exceptionally important decision. Having known Mr. Banjac from before, I sincerely doubted that such an idea could be his own and that he was in the position to think along these lines because such a policy had already been established and outlined at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned "higher bodies." Could you further specify what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS in Kljuc had to go to the Serbian Autonomous Region and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina whenever some decisions or the implementation of such decisions was in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you've described earlier in your evidence the very close association you had with Mr. Banjac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I see your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you've described in your early -- your evidence the very close association that you had with Mr. Banjac. Were you aware of occasions when Mr. Banjac visited higher-level members of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would attend meetings; however, I did not discuss that with him. I didn't ask him where he went. I know that he went to Banja Luka. I know that because he would ask me to sign his travel orders for Banja Luka. I had to sign those for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did he go to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we went to Sarajevo together up to September or October 1991. After that, he didn't go there. Whenever he needed to establish some contacts, he would go to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did higher-level members of the SDS party visit Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some did. Mr. Nikola Koljevic, who was a member of the Presidency; there was one such meeting that I attended in my capacity as the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. On one occasion, Radovan Karadzic also visited us, but I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When did these visits take place?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic came in the first half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Karadzic visited?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic came a lot later, but I can't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you recall what was discussed at either of those meetings, with either Mr. Koljevic or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was discussed at the meeting with Karadzic. As for Mr. Koljevic, during that meeting, while I was there, the discussion was along the most general lines, the development and growth of the municipality, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I'd like to refer you back to the document that's before you, in particular page 3 of that document. You'll see approximately -- just above the middle of the page there is a reference to "Strategic goals formulated at a meeting in Banja Luka." It states that "These goals were presented at that meeting." I'd like you to read the first goal, goal number 1, that is, "There must be a state separation of the three national communities," and tell me whether that goal was implemented in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How was that goal implemented?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the following way: There was a complete takeover of power by the SDS and the Municipality of Kljuc was linked to the SAO Krajina, which was part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Practically for the Muslim citizens, how did that -- the implementation of that goal affect them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lost their jobs. They were terrified by the situation. They no longer had a vision as to how things would end. They were deprived of their rights, because they had lost the most important thing that any individual is entitled to, and that is their right to work. Later on they were expelled from the area, which after that has become completely ethnically clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. That ends my questions in respect of this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll -- and how much time would you still need? We had in the beginning -- you had an assessment, anything between six and eight hours. I think we're now at approximately six, a little bit over six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will do everything possible to finish in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it would come to any questions about conditions and circumstances in the Manjaca camp, which I can imagine on the basis of the 65 ter summary, I'd draw your attention to the fact that while the previous witness was examined, that there seemed not to be major disagreement to -- between the parties. So I would like to cut that really short and I might even intervene myself. But that should really take not much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, please proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness be presented with the next exhibit, which is the second-last exhibit on the second page with the English translation Y0018557.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would get number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be 245 and 245.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, prior to arriving in The Hague recently, had you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document when I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is a statement from Omer Filipovic. And on the last page, it is dated 29 May 1992. Where was Omer Filipovic on the 29th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that date, Omer Filipovic was at the police administration of Kljuc or Gradiska, I don't know precisely, in prison, in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, have you had an opportunity since you arrived in The Hague to read this statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in general terms, to the best of your knowledge, and to the matters that you have knowledge on, is this statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the greatest part of the statement, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you refer to page 3 of the statement, and in particular to the paragraph that starts -- the last paragraph on -- in -- on page 3, which goes over to page 4. There's a reference there to a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just have the first few words of the paragraph, because it's been located in the B/C/S version, but for those of us in the English version, just the first two or three words would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the third page of the English version and it attempts -- it commences: "I attempted to copy the organisation of the existing staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: There's a reference to you in this paragraph, Mr. Egrlic, and it states that you were a member of the TO staff and supposed to perform the political functions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, if we refer back -- no, actually, if we refer to the first paragraph appearing on page 3 and to five lines down - and in the English version, this is the second page, and it's commencing four lines up from the bottom - there's a reference to a directive for impeding military columns, and it states that Mr. Filipovic informed you, Mr. Egrlic, about the contents of the directive. Is that correct? Did he inform you about that directive?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct, and I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Having read this a couple of days ago, do any other matters occur to you in this document that you consider to be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one thing. As far as the Territorial Defence is concerned, Mr. Filipovic is talking mainly about the strength and the level of organisation. The Territorial Defence was mainly a concept, an idea to be implemented. It never reached the stage of actually lining up the members and inspecting the troops and the state of their military equipment, their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: There are references to various Muslim settlements in this document that are located north of Kljuc. Were you aware that there were people who were assigned guard duty in the settlements?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there were village guards from the beginning of 1992 onwards, in view of the deteriorated security situations. We discussed this at one of the sessions of the Municipal Assembly and took the stand that monitoring should be organised, as well as village guards, because some individuals had already made raids on villages with the aim of robbery, and the idea was to prevent such raids in the future and protect the villages from such raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'll now ask you some questions about matters that are referred to in this document, but it won't be necessary for you to refer to the document to provide your answer, but feel free to do so if you would wish to. Was Omer Filipovic appointed by the commander of the Territorial Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Colonel Hasan Efendic, to be the commander of the TO Staff of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did Omer Filipovic form that TO Staff and was it based in Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in consultation with you, did Omer Filipovic set out some proposed organisation of that staff in the general region north of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk about it. He, as a reserve lieutenant, was supposed to develop some sort of organisational scheme for their headquarters, for their staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did he refer to the employee of the Municipal Assembly, Iksan Zukanovic, to assist him with this organisation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were you aware whether or not a number of men who were approached to participate in the TO were too scared to do so?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that, because I don't know whom he had asked and how they responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Is it consistent with your knowledge at the time that, all in all, there was a potential for a unit of about 1200 to 1300 men to be formed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hypothetically, yes, because there were men of appropriate age who could have become members of the TO. However, the prevailing circumstances and the situation I have already described did not make it possible to perform a proper mobilisation and to put together units in the way that is common in military practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In terms of the weapons available to these men, would there have been approximately 800 weapons of various kinds?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, because there was no depot from which weapons were issued, nor had there ever been an inspection to establish how many weapons there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, was there an incident in Crljeni, a Muslim settlement north of Kljuc, where approximately eight soldiers were captured?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the village of Crljeni, C-r-l-j-a-n-i [as interpreted]. There was an incident which occurred when seven to eight soldiers entered the village with specific intentions. However, the village guards were alert, and these people were captured and later released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were they Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did Omer Filipovic meet with you and discuss this issue with you and subsequently did you speak with Jovo Banjac about this incident?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic discussed this incident on several occasions, as far as I know, with Mr. Banjac and Mr. Kondic, and these soldiers were released in good health.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You stated earlier that Mr. Filipovic was very -- a very good friend of Vinko Kondic, and Mr. Filipovic in his statement here says, in fact, that he and Vinko Kondic were like brothers since childhood. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, did Omer Filipovic contact Vinko Kondic and did he travel with Vinko Kondic around villages in the north of Kljuc in order to settle down any situation that could have been developing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In my previous question, I mentioned the 26th of May. It may be the 27th of May that I should have referred to, but in or around the 26th of May did he do that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, in the morning I was in Pudin Han. Then I went to see my family, which had already fled together with other families from the settlement where they used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was occurring in the settlement where they used to live?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Egrlici, Sehici, and Drezovici [phoen] were targeted with gunfire, and they were afraid that the army would soon enter these settlements, so they fled to the woods about 5 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What happened to you on the 27th of May from the morning until the evening?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, I was in Pudin Han. Then I went to the place to which my family had fled. And when I returned to my office in Pudin Han, I realised that an incident had occurred in an area called Busije, involving an exchange of fire between the army and the local village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And what did you do in respect of that incident?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing to be done about it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What happened on the 28th of May?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, since I was unable to go home because I had no home any more, I spent the night in a house in Pudin Han, and in the morning of the 28th of May I had an accident. I shot myself from a pistol. And when I tried to get to a hospital, I was stopped at a checkpoint just outside the town and I was escorted to the police station in Kljuc, and from then on to the Stara Gradiska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, we'll deal with that matter in a few moments. Just can you explain to me how it was you came to shoot yourself in the foot.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before, scared as I was of the situation, I put a bullet in the barrel without fastening the safety lock, and the next morning I took my jacket with the pocket -- with the gun inside the pocket, and the pistol fell out and fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness two exhibits, two documents. The first one is one that is fourth up on the second page of the exhibit list, and it's dated 28 May 1992, and the translation ERN is 01107557. And the other one is on the top page of -- the top of the third page of the exhibit list; it's dated 10 June 1992, and the ERN is 00914852. If the 10 June document could be marked and shown to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 10th of June document would be 246, original, and 246.1, translation; and the 29th of May -- the 28th of May, 1992 document would be -- would be 247 for the original and 247.1 for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, can you look at the document which is in handwriting. Do you have that document before you? And purports to be handwritten notes from the Kljuc police station. Can you look at item 2 on the second page of that document, which is headed "Staff TO," and can you confirm that that accurately describes the staff of the Territorial Defence that we have previously referred to.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In respect of the other positions and listings in this document, do you have any knowledge of these matters?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what your question refers to, but as it regards the Crisis Staff, which is listed here as a body that existed, it was only an idea and it never took off the ground because it was never confirmed by the Municipal Council -- better, say the deputies who were members of the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc. As for the other listings, in my view this is just an outline as to what could be organised, in view of the fact that there were human resources available, in view of their age and their obligation to be part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I'd like you to refer to the next document, which is the order dated 28 May 1992 of the Kljuc Crisis Staff. Can you tell me what occurred following this order? And for the record, this is an order in respect of the surrender of weapons and a call to the decent and loyal Muslims living in the area to contribute to a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was followed through. Units of the Serbian army entered various settlements. What ensued was that the majority of the population was brought in for interrogation. Some of the weapons were found. A large number of the population was detained in the schools and thereafter deported into the Manjaca camp. During that same period of time, there were a number of killings and mass execution of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could Mr. Egrlic be presented with the next exhibit, which is the one that appears on the list on page 2, dated 1 May 1992, and the ERN is 03023558. It's the rather large handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would get number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P248 and P248.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I not already have 248? The handwritten document, the previous one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the previous one was 247, which was the Crisis Staff order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We concur with that, Your Honour. That's where we believe we've got to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then I indicated that wrong, yes. Then I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, can you take a look through this document and tell me whether you recognise any of the handwriting in this document.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time when I arrived here. I recognised the Cyrillic handwriting on page 1. This is Vinko Kondic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you refer to page 1, could you read out the numbers, the eight-digit number sequence of the page you're referring to. That's the sequence that's stamped on top on the page.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is 00574398.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So in the document that you have before you, you recognise the handwriting on the page that has the heading "Number 1." Can you scan backwards through the document. In respect of the preceding two page, do you recognise the handwriting on those pages? That is, from the number 00574396. Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The page is 00574399. This is the number on the -- on the next page, and the handwriting is the same as on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I think the question was about the preceding, not the following pages, though I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So would you please look at the last two digits 96 and 97, so the previous pages. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the handwriting is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that is the handwriting of Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In respect of the handwriting that appears on the pages that precede the pages you have identified, that is, from the first page of the document through to the page concluding with the digits "95," do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the handwriting is the same. This is Vinko Kondic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question. If you would look at the page with the last two digits "88." You see there's an upper part -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have an upper part. You have a empty middle part, and then a lower part. Is this all Vinko Kondic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure about the top part, but the bottom part is in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether it was all Vinko Kondic's handwriting. I mean, there are other people who can write Cyrillic script, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there are, but what is written in the Cyrillic script I recognise as Vinko Kondic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the non-Cyrillic, on the top of the page, which would -- seems to be quite similar to what we find on the previous pages and which also seems to be quite similar to what we find on 93 and 94?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This looks like -- like it, judging by the lower part of the letters; however, having worked with Mr. Vinko Kondic in the Sana construction company, I had a lot of opportunities to see his handwriting in the Cyrillic script. As for the Latinic script, I'm not sure that this is his handwriting; although, there are similarities, especially when it comes to the lower portion of the letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I refer you to the page that ends with the numbers "98" and has the heading "Number 1." In particular, I refer you to the last paragraph on that page, which continues over to the page with the last two digits "99." If you look down at the last paragraph, that paragraph commences - and correct me if I'm wrong - that paragraph commences: "There are not many Croats on the territory of the municipality"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In this paragraph, Mr. Kondic writes that "The Muslims in the municipality are well organised." And we've dealt with the issue of your organisation, so I don't need you to respond to that particular matter. However, if you turn over the page, you will see on the page marked "99," that the final sentence of Mr. Kondic's report concludes: "It is realistic to assume that the Muslim and Croatian forces cannot have even an initial advantage but their activities may initially cause confusion in our ranks." How do you respond to that assessment of the Muslim capability when assessed by reference to the strength of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a good assessment, given the fact that the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Kljuc was neither organised nor prepared well enough to wage any kind of war, and they knew it only too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I've finished with that document. You have heard His Honour state before the previous break that we don't need to receive from you very specific details of your detention in the various facilities and what occurred, but if you could, without my further prompting, just run through a brief chronology of where you were detained after the 28th of May, who detained you, and if you were subject to any beatings or other activities or witnessed beatings and other activities, could you note those for the Trial Chamber and could you note your observations in respect of what occurred to other people you were detained with.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of May, when I was arrested at the checkpoint close to the town, I was taken to the police administration of Kljuc. There I was beaten. In addition to the wound that I had already sustained, I had various injuries on my head and on my body, and in that state I was transferred to the Kljuc hospital, where I stayed for a while. During the day, around 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon, I was in the hospital, and then I was again taken to the police administration building in an ambulance. In front of the building and in front of the car where I was, I saw a truck with a canvas cover. This truck was driving in front of us as we drove off in the direction of Banja Luka. In the hospital, I had been told that we would transferred to the Banja Luka hospital; however, we never even stopped in Banja Luka but, rather, proceeded towards Gradiska. As we were leaving Banja Luka, during the night the truck and the ambulance pulled over. Soldiers from the Logor barracks came and I was beaten by them again, half conscious and covered in blood. I saw people on the truck. They were being thrown out of the truck with their hands tied behind their back -- backs. Those people were beaten heavily and then again loaded onto the truck. We set off again and arrived in the Stara Gradiska prison. I was detained in one of the cells there together with another man, who was unconscious. After a day or two, he was taken away. Later on I found out that he succumbed to his wounds. I was transferred to another cell, where I stayed for some 15 days or so, and then I was transferred to the Manjaca camp, where I stayed for a few months and where, like everybody else there, I was exposed to various forms of torture, beating, humiliation, deprivation of food and water, and other such things. When the Manjaca camp was about to be dismantled under the pressure of the international general public and the Red Cross, 531 of us were transferred to the Batkovici camp near Bijeljina. I stayed there until the 29th of January, 2003, and then I was liberated, I was set free in an exchange that took place in Orasje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few additional questions, then. Were the circumstances in Batkovici camp similar to the ones in Manjaca camp? Or were they different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were similar. The only difference being the fact in Manjaca we were accommodated in cow sheds. We lie on the floor, on the concrete floor on a very thin straw mattress; whereas, in Batkovici, this mattress was somewhat thicker. It was a mat. And the control was not so strict, or better say the treatment of the military police who controlled the camp was somewhat better. There was less beating. Fewer people would be called out during the night. We had better access to water. We had an exterior faucet, so we could wash our faces. We did not have all that in Manjaca. The conditions were somewhat better and somewhat more bearable in Batkovici. Still, having said that, both camps were very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for Manjaca, did you see anyone dying in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I saw several people dying. I saw several people being beaten. I saw several people being exhausted from starvation. A lot of people became sick. I saw all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer to be that it was due to the circumstances and due to the beatings that people were dying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as guards are concerned, who was guarding Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many, and they were the Serbian military police. Some of them ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "some of them." We didn't hear what the following words were, if you spoke them. What would you like to tell us in respect of some of these Serbian military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that I knew some of them by name, the way they introduced themselves and the way others introduced them. I learned some of their names or their nicknames. One of them was Spaga. That was his nickname. I don't know his name. He discharged the duties of the commander of that police force that was guarding the camp. Another one was Zeljko Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment the names are not of greater importance. About the Stara Gradiska camp, was the situation there close to Manjaca or rather closer to what you said, the slightly better conditions in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stara Gradiska was nothing like Manjaca or Batkovici. It was a building that had always been a prison, and it had purpose-built cells where detainees were kept. I was in one of those cells; whereas, others were in bigger cells which could hold up to 30 people. Actually, there were up to 30 people in the cell; although, the capacity, the normal capacity of those cells was only up to five, six people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of food, water, sanitary situation, was it better or worse than Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation was worse when it came to sanitary situation because we were humiliated; we experienced all sorts of humiliation when we had to go and relieve ourselves, because every time we wanted to do that, we would be beaten, and the time we had at our disposal would be limited to three to five minutes. As far as the food was concerned, it was somewhat better than in Manjaca. We received water to a somewhat greater amount. In Manjaca, we did not have any access to water. The detainees in Manjaca would bring water in jerrycans from -- from a nearby lake. Very often there would be tadpoles swimming in that water. The quality of that water was really poor, but still the detainees had to drink it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Any further questions, Mr. Margetts? I notice that I'm guilty of that as well, that we are far over the time already, 12 minutes. If it's a matter of one minute, I would ask the interpreters to stay with us for that one minute. If it would be more, we have to resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Just one question on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But we will -- we want the show a video, which will take probably about 15 minutes, and I have a couple -- or about three or four more documents. So I expect that we would like to run for about 20 or 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We couldn't do it now because for all kind of practical reasons and also since we have been sitting four hours today and there's a Plenary of the Judges this afternoon, so we couldn't stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: However, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- could I just ask one question in respect of Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, what happened to Omer Filipovic in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Manjaca, Omer Filipovic was killed in a very cruel way; he had been tortured for days and died in great pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one further matter, and that is that the witness referred to his detention as lasting until 2003, and that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We noticed that. You said you were exchanged in 2003. May I take it that -- I think you said January 2003. May I take it that you meant to refer to 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clarified for the record as well. Then we'll adjourn. We'll not resume tomorrow morning, but we'll resume tomorrow in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00. Mr. Egrlic, may I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony given and still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon. Mr. Registrar, do we know in what courtroom? Will it also be Courtroom I? Well, the parties should inform themselves whether it will be in Courtroom I or any of the other courtrooms, unless you would know immediately, Mr. -- It's no problem. The parties will find the courtroom where we are sitting, and if we are missing one, we will just wait until they're there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in Courtroom I. I again would like to thank very much the interpreters for having given their extra time. Just for their consolation, the recess will be next week, so no abuse of your cooperation could be made any more at that very moment. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of July, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
